content: African trypanosomiasis, also known as sleeping sickness, is a parasitic disease affecting both humans and animals. It is caused by protozoa of the genus Trypanosoma and is transmitted through the bite of the tsetse fly. The disease is endemic to regions of Sub-Saharan Africa, affecting approximately 36 countries and 60 million people. The clinical progression of human African trypanosomiasis occurs in two distinct stages. In the first stage, the parasite is present in the peripheral circulation but has not yet invaded the central nervous system (CNS). Once the parasite crosses the blood-brain barrier and infects the CNS, the disease progresses to the second stage. The rate of disease progression and clinical manifestations depend on the subspecies of the parasite causing the infection, either Trypanosoma brucei rhodesiense or Trypanosoma brucei gambiense. Without treatment, infection with either subspecies will ultimately result in coma and death. African trypanosomiasis has been present in Africa for thousands of years. In 1903, David Bruce identified the causative agent and its vector. By 1910, the differentiation between the subspecies of the protozoa was established. The disease can be classified into two types based on the pathogen and geographic location: East African trypanosomiasis and West African trypanosomiasis. African trypanosomiasis is caused by protozoan hemoflagellates belonging to the Trypanosoma brucei complex. Transmission to humans typically occurs through the bite of an infected tsetse fly. A trypanosomal chancre often develops at the site of inoculation. This is followed by a hemolymphatic stage, characterized by symptoms such as fever, lymphadenopathy, and pruritus. In the meningoencephalitic stage, CNS invasion can lead to headaches, somnolence, abnormal behavior, loss of consciousness, and coma. The course of infection is more acute with Trypanosoma brucei rhodesiense than with Trypanosoma brucei gambiense. Clinical symptoms generally appear within 1–3 weeks of the infectious bite for T. b. rhodesiense and months to years for T. b. gambiense. The hemolymphatic stage of African trypanosomiasis presents with symptoms such as rash, fever, and anemia, which must be differentiated from other diseases like brucellosis, typhoid fever, malaria, tuberculosis, lymphoma, dengue, and leptospirosis. In the neurological stage, mental status changes and sleep disturbances are prominent, necessitating differential diagnoses that include CNS tuberculosis, meningitis, and HIV-related opportunistic infections such as cryptococcal meningitis. The annual prevalence of African trypanosomiasis is currently estimated to be less than 20,000 cases. In 2014, 3,796 cases of sleeping sickness were reported to the World Health Organization, with Trypanosoma brucei gambiense accounting for over 98% of cases. The disease does not show a preference for any specific age group. Risk factors for African trypanosomiasis include residence in endemic regions of Central or South America, living in old houses with mud and stick walls or straw roofs, ingestion of contaminated water, or receiving blood transfusions or organ donations from individuals in high-endemicity areas. The risk of infection increases with repeated tsetse fly bites. Neonates are at higher risk if breastfed by infected mothers with bleeding or cracked nipples or if born to seropositive mothers with active disease. If left untreated, African trypanosomiasis leads to progressive and irreversible mental deterioration, ultimately resulting in death. Common complications include anemia, aspiration pneumonia, meningoencephalitis, seizures, coma, perinatal death, or abortion due to congenital infection. With treatment, the prognosis is good, but without treatment, the mortality rate approaches 100%. The diagnosis of African trypanosomiasis relies on demonstrating trypanosomes through microscopic examination of chancre fluid, lymph node aspirates, blood, bone marrow, or cerebrospinal fluid in the late stages of infection. Imaging studies such as X-rays, CT scans, MRI, and ultrasound do not provide diagnostic findings for this disease. Medical treatment should begin as soon as possible and is guided by the patient’s symptoms and laboratory results. Medications are the cornerstone of treatment. Pentamidine isethionate and suramin are the drugs of choice for the hemolymphatic stages of West and East African trypanosomiasis, respectively. Melarsoprol is the preferred treatment for late-stage disease with CNS involvement caused by either T. b. gambiense or T. b. rhodesiense. Hospitalization is required during the second stage of the disease, and periodic follow-up exams, including spinal taps, are necessary for two years. Without medical treatment, death occurs within weeks to months. Surgical intervention is not recommended for managing African trypanosomiasis. Primary prevention focuses on eradicating the tsetse fly vector. Strategies include the use of insecticides, improved construction materials for walls and roofs, and testing of blood and organ donations. Regular active surveillance, involving case detection and treatment alongside tsetse fly control, is essential for controlling sleeping sickness. Secondary prevention strategies are identical to primary prevention measures.
